paper.title: Differences Between Urban and Rural Counties in Pregnancy-Related Deaths - United States, 2015-2024.
paper.summary: Residents of rural communities face multiple health challenges, including higher pregnancy-related mortality (the death of a woman during or within 1 year of the end of pregnancy from any cause related to or aggravated by pregnancy); however, causes of pregnancy-related mortality by urban-rural classification are not well described. To better understand differences in pregnancy-related mortality by urban-rural classification levels, CDC analyzed data from 7,357 pregnancy-related deaths that occurred during 2015-2024 from CDC's Pregnancy Mortality Surveillance System. The numbers of pregnancy-related deaths per 100,000 live births, or pregnancy-related mortality ratios (PRMRs), were examined across six urban-rural classifications based on the National Center for Health Statistics' urban-rural classification scheme, and by race and ethnicity, age, and underlying cause of death. Although most deaths occurred among women living in urban counties, PRMRs were highest among those living in rural counties across age categories, most racial and ethnic groups, and cause-of-death categories. Cardiovascular conditions (including cardiomyopathy) and infection or sepsis were the most frequent causes of pregnancy-related mortality across all urban-rural classifications. These findings highlight potential needs to improve access to primary, obstetric, and specialty care in rural communities.

paper.title: Notes from the Field: Death Involving the Semisynthetic Kratom-Derived Opioid Dihydro-7-Hydroxymitragynine (MGM-15) from a Product Labeled Cat's Claw - San Francisco, California, September 2026.
paper.summary: At 7:30 a.m. on September 22, 2026, a man aged 37 years was found unresponsive by his partner in his residence in San Francisco, California. He was asystolic when emergency medical services (EMS) arrived and was pronounced dead by EMS at the scene. A prominent foam cone at the decedent's mouth and nares, constricted pupils, and vomitus suggested central nervous system and respiratory depression preceding death. Because death was suspected to have occurred >1 hour before EMS arrived, no resuscitation efforts were made, and naloxone was not administered. Investigators from the San Francisco Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) recovered an empty four-tablet blister card labeled as Uncaria tomentosa (cat's claw) extract, 100 mg per tablet, sold as Script Botanicals x Maui Laboratories Paradise Blend* (Figure); no other evidence of substance use was observed at the scene.

paper.title: Social media and adolescent mental health: Why screen time is no longer the question?
paper.summary: Children's and adolescents' exposure to social media has reached such a scale that the debate over whether they should be online has become moot. In Argentina, the average age at which children get their first personal phone with internet access is 9.6 years, and eight out of ten adolescents use social media every day. There remains genuine disagreement among researchers regarding the impact on mental health: while some authors argue that the widespread adoption of smartphones has reshaped childhood and accounts for the rise in anxiety, depression, and self-harm, others show that the effect on the general population is very small. This update proposes a way to resolve the contradiction in practice: abandon duration of use as a risk criterion and structure clinical evaluation around patterns of use and individual vulnerability. Restricting access reduces exposure, but does not, on its own, improve mental health.

paper.title: Perceived Gesture Dynamics in Nonverbal Expression of Emotion
paper.summary: Recent judgment studies have shown that people are able to fairly correctly attribute emotional states to others' bodily expressions. It is, however, not clear which movement qualities are salient, and how this applies to emotional gesture during speech-based interaction. In this study we investigated how the expression of emotions that vary on three major emotion dimensions—that is, arousal, valence, and potency—affects the perception of dynamic arm gestures. Ten professional actors enacted 12 emotions in a scenario-based social interaction setting. Participants (N = 43) rated all emotional expressions with muted sound and blurred faces on six spatiotemporal characteristics of gestural arm movement that were found to be related to emotion in previous research (amount of movement, movement speed, force, fluency, size, and height/vertical position). Arousal and potency were found to be strong determinants of the perception of gestural dynamics, whereas the differences between positive or negative emotions were less pronounced. These results confirm the importance of arm movement in communicating major emotion dimensions and show that gesture forms an integrated part of multimodal nonverbal emotion communication.

paper.title: Feeding Your Feelings: Emotion Regulation Strategies and Emotional Eating
paper.summary: The process by which emotions affect eating behavior emerges as one of the central unresolved questions in the field of emotional eating. The present studies address the hypothesis that the regulation strategies people use to deal with these emotions are responsible for increased eating. Negative emotions were induced and intake of comfort food and non—comfort food was measured by means of taste tests. Emotion induction was preceded by measuring individual differences in emotion regulation strategies (Study 1) or by instructions to regulate emotions in either an adaptive (reappraisal) or maladaptive (suppression) manner (Study 2). Study 3 also entailed a control condition without any regulation instructions. Relative to reappraisal and spontaneous expression, suppression led to increased food intake, but only of the comfort foods. Emotions themselves were not responsible for this effect. These findings provide new evidence that the way in which emotions are regulated affects eating behavior.
